Harmonic Mean

FractionsArithmeticPhysics
Game: Watch a relay race: every runner covers the same distance, but each one may run at a different speed.
How to play: Drag the highlighted bar or use the up and down arrow keys to change that leg's speed. Choose a number of legs, switch the bar view, then press Race!
Look for the math

Two trips can have the same start, the same finish and the same two speeds, yet different average speeds. The difference is whether you spend the same time at each speed or cover the same distance at each speed. This applet is the equal-distance case.

One hour each, or half the road each?

In the first problem on the page a driver goes 20 mph for one hour and 30 mph for the next hour. The distances are 20 and 30 miles, so the arithmetic mean gives the answer: (20 + 30)/2 = 25 mph. In the second problem the first half of the road is driven at 20 mph and the second half at 30 mph. If each half is d miles, the time is d/20 + d/30 hours and the whole trip is 2d miles. Its average speed is 2d/(d/20 + d/30) = 2/(1/20 + 1/30) = 24 mph, not 25.

Equal distances make the reciprocals add

With N legs of the same length, each leg takes 1/v units of time at speed v. Total time is 1/v1 + ... + 1/vN and total distance is N, so the steady speed that covers the whole course in the same time is

S = N / (1/v1 + 1/v2 + ... + 1/vN)

That is exactly the harmonic mean of the leg speeds; for two speeds it is H(a,b) = 2ab/(a+b). The test compares the applet's own Evaluate() arithmetic with this formula for every leg count from 2 to 40, checks all 100 pairs and all 1,000 triples of whole-number speeds from 1 to 10, and confirms the page's claim that the arithmetic mean is never smaller than the harmonic mean, with equality only when all the speeds are equal.

Why the twins finish with the relay team

The chart at the bottom plots distance against time. The relay team's broken line rises steeply on a fast leg and gently on a slow one; the twins' straight line has slope S. At the end of leg k the relay has covered k miles after tk = 1/v1 + ... + 1/vk hours, while the twins are at S·tk. Either team may be ahead in between. At the common finish tN = N/S, the twins are at S·tN = N, so they tie without ever changing speed. The upper bars use the same times: in T vs V a slow leg is wider because it takes longer, and in Dist vs V every leg is equally wide because every leg is equally long.

A different page from the sangaku applets

The address in the applet archive points to Bogomolny's geometry article, which lists lengths equal to the harmonic mean in a semicircle, a trapezoid, an inscribed square and an 1877 sangaku (CP = H(a,b)/2). The applet itself is embedded on Averages, Arithmetic and Harmonic Means, where the claim is the equal-distance speed result above. Those geometric lengths belong to the separate HarmonicMeanSangaku and HarmonicRatio applets (the latter constructs AE = H(b,c) with an angle bisector); this port follows the applet and its own page. The race animation is continuous here rather than the original one-pixel step every 100 milliseconds, and the page's 1-to-10 speed sliders and 2-to-40 leg range are unchanged.

Try 20 mph and 30 mph in two legs, then press Race! and watch which team leads at the first leg and which team is level at the finish.
